description: Download the Mox compiler, install clang on Linux or Windows, and check that everything works.
text: Before you write any code, you need two things: the Mox compiler and a linker. This page shows how to get both.

heading: Download the compiler
text: Get the latest zip from GitHub releases. One zip has the compiler for Windows and Linux (x86_64) and the base modules. Unpack it anywhere. Keep the compiler executable in the same folder as the modules folder. The compiler looks for modules next to itself. You can add this folder to your PATH, so you can type mox from any place.

heading: Why you need a linker
text: Mox does not have its own linker. It compiles your code to an .obj file, then calls an outside linker to make an executable. By default this linker is clang. You can use another one, see Linking.

heading: Linux
text: Install clang: If you see a version GLIBCXX_* not found error, update libstdc++: Some prebuilt libraries in modules/vendor need a newer glibc. The simplest fix is to update your system. You can also build those libraries yourself.

heading: Windows
text: On Windows you need clang and the system libraries it links with. There are two ways.

heading: Option 1: MSYS2 (recommended)
text: This uses MinGW clang from MSYS2. With the script: press Win+R, type powershell.exe -ExecutionPolicy Bypass and press Enter. Go to the Mox folder and run: Or by hand, in PowerShell: Then add C:\msys64\ucrt64\bin to your PATH.

heading: Option 2: MSVC clang
text: This is slower to install and uses Visual Studio Build Tools. With the script: press Win+R, type powershell.exe -ExecutionPolicy Bypass and press Enter. Go to the Mox folder and run: Or by hand: With this option, two things are important: Always build from the x64 Native Tools Command Prompt (find it in the Start menu). Or run vcvars64.bat first, it is in C:\Program Files (x86)\Microsoft Visual Studio\18\BuildTools\VC\Auxiliary\Build\. Always pass llvm_target_triple="x86_64-pc-windows-msvc" to the compiler.

heading: Check that it works
text: Run: It prints the compiler version and all options. If you see this list, the compiler is ready. Next: Hello world.

description: Write, build and run your first Mox program.
text: This is the smallest Mox program that prints something. Make sure you did the setup first.

heading: The program
text: Save this as hello.mox: Line by line: import "std.mox"; loads the standard module. It has println and many other helpers. #linkc gives the function a plain C name. The C runtime calls main, so it must have a C name. println prints a line. Each {} in the text is replaced with the next value from the list .{ ... }.

heading: Build and run
text: Pass the file to the compiler: The compiler makes hello.mox.obj, then calls clang to link it into hello.mox.exe. Run it: It prints hello world!. To choose the output name and turn on optimizations:

heading: Comments
text: Next: Compiler options.

description: Pick a backend, turn on optimizations and debug info, and set output paths.
text: Run mox help to see every option. This page covers the ones you will use most. Most options are written as name=value. A few short flags (-O3, -g, -o) work like in other compilers.

heading: Backends
text: Mox has three backends: jit - the default. A fast x86_64 backend. Good while you develop. llvm - slower to compile, makes faster code. Can target other platforms. c - outputs C source code. Pick one with backend=:

heading: Optimizations
text: -O0 uses the jit backend. -O1, -O2, -O3 use LLVM with that optimization level.

heading: Debug info
text: -g writes DWARF debug info, so you can use a debugger. It also turns on embed_source_paths=true.

heading: Output paths
text: -o=path sets the path of the final executable. out=path sets the path of the compiler output (the .obj file, LLVM IR or C source).

heading: Other useful options
text: compile="./hello.mox" - another way to pass the main file. linker=... - the linker command. See Linking. llvm_target_triple=... - target for the LLVM backend, for example x86_64-pc-windows-msvc. llvm_out_format=obj|ir|asm|bitcode - what LLVM writes. modules_dir=... - where to look for modules. By default it is the modules folder next to the compiler.

heading: Placeholders
text: Some options can use placeholders. The compiler replaces them: :MOX_LINKER_OUT: - the executable path (from -o, or the main file name + .exe) :MOX_COMPILER_DIR: - the folder of the compiler :MOX_COMPILE_ROOT_DIR: - the folder of the main file :MOX_WORKING_DIR: - the current folder :MOX_COMPILER_OUT: - the compiler output path

description: How Mox calls the linker, how to use your own linker, and how to link libraries from code.
text: Mox compiles your code to an .obj file. An outside linker turns it into an executable. This page shows how that works and how to change it.

heading: The default linker command
text: The default is: So when you run: the compiler builds example.mox.obj and then runs: The compiler adds the .obj file and any libraries to the end of the command. It expects the linker to add the C runtime by itself, and clang does.

heading: Use another linker
text: Pass your own command:

heading: Link by hand
text: Turn the linker off. The compiler will only write the .obj file: Then link it with any tool you like.

heading: Link libraries from code
text: You can add to the linker command from Mox code. This runs at compile time with #run (more about it in Compile time). __compiler_link_lib adds a library with -l. Write the name without .a, .lib, .dll or .so: The linker command becomes: If the second argument is true, the compiler loads the library into itself. Then you can call its functions at compile time. See Build scripts in code. __compiler_append_linker adds any text to the command:

heading: Problems on Windows
text: If you installed clang by hand, you also need the Windows SDK and VC Tools. They come with Visual Studio. If you get a strange linker error: Build with linker=false and try to link the .obj file by hand first. If MSVC clang can not find system libraries, run it from the x64 Native Tools Command Prompt, or run vcvarsall.bat x64 first. You can also give the paths by hand: Or install MSYS2 clang, see Setup. With MSVC clang, always pass llvm_target_triple="x86_64-pc-windows-msvc" to the compiler.

description: Declare variables, use the basic types, structs, enums, arrays, slices and strings.

heading: Declaring variables
text: A variable is written as name : type = value: If you skip the type, it comes from the value: Every variable must have a initial value. This is an error:

heading: Basic types
text: signed integers: i8, i16, i32, i64, i128 unsigned integers: u8, u16, u32, u64, u128 floats: f32, f64 bool void A number can have its type at the end: A number without a type is a compile time number. Math on such numbers is done by the compiler. When it is stored into a real type, the compiler checks that the value fits without loss.

heading: Zero and garbage
text: 0 sets any value to zeros (zeroing memory): If you really want to skip the initial value (for speed), say it out loud with #memory_garbage: Mox follows idea of ZII - Zero Is Initialization. So better design your data in a way that zero is a valid default state.

heading: Structs
text: The memory layout of a struct is the same as in C. Struct values are written with .{ }. Fields can be named. Use , or ; between them: Fields could also come just in order: When the type is known, you can write just .{ ... }. Otherwise put the type in front: MyStruct.{ ... }.

heading: Enums
text: By default an enum uses the smallest integer type that fits all values. You can set it with : u8 and set values with :=.

heading: Arrays
text: An array holds its items inside itself. When you copy an array, all items are copied. a.ptr gives a pointer to the first item.a.len gives length of an array. It is "synthetic" fields that works as operators, in memory only items are stored for fixed arrays.

heading: Slices
text: A slice is a pointer and a length, like struct { ptr: *T; len: i64; }. When you copy a slice, only the pointer and length are copied, not the items.

heading: Strings
text: A string literal can be one of two things, based on the type: Most Mox code uses []u8. Use *u8 when you call C functions. String literals are null terminated but Mox code relies on string slices without null termination.In case you need to pass string to some C API that expects null terminated string, use #temp_c_string.

heading: Constants
text: A constant is known at compile time. Any initial value or expression for constants are evaluated at compile time.

heading: Global variables
text: A variable declared outside of functions is global. Its initial value is also evaluated at compile time, the same way as for const. The result is stored in the program, so no code runs for it at start: Unlike a constant, a global can be changed while the program runs.

heading: Two special types
text: Mox has two more built-in types. They are used for compile time code: __type_ptr - a type as a value. Every type in Mox is a __type_ptr. __ast_ptr - a piece of code as a value. You will see them in Generics and Code generation.

description: Math, comparison, bit operations, casts, vector math with swizzling and the pipe operator.

heading: Math and comparison
text: Compound assignment works too: There is no operator overloading.

heading: Comparing structs and arrays
text: == on structs, arrays and slices compares field by field, item by item. Two slices with the same items are equal, even if they point to different memory: If slice's ptr and len are equal, there is no item by item comparison as they are the same slice.

heading: Casts
text: .cast(type) converts a value:

heading: Bit operations
text: Shifts and other bit tools are built-in functions:

heading: Overflow
text: By default +, - and * expect that overflow never happens. If you want numbers to wrap around, say so:

heading: Vector math
text: Math works on arrays of 2 to 4 items, like vectors in 3D math. You can also read and write parts of them with xyzw or rgba letters (this is called swizzling): These are normal arrays. They just have these extra operators. Swizzling does not work on arrays with more than 4 items.

heading: Pipe operator
text: |> passes the value on the left as the first argument of the call on the right: is the same as:

description: Take an address, read through a pointer, access fields and move pointers by bytes.
text: Mox has raw pointers, like C. There is no garbage collector.

heading: Taking an address and reading
text: .^ takes a pointer. .* reads the value it points to.

heading: Fields through a pointer
text: You do not need a special operator. Use . like with a normal value:

heading: Null pointer
text: Like any other type, a pointer can be set to 0. This makes it null: When there is no type to infer from, use the nullptr function. It makes a null pointer of the given type:

heading: Moving a pointer
text: There is no p + 1 for pointers. Use these helpers from the standard modules: They read well with the pipe operator:

heading: Pointer to a slice
text: slice(ptr, len) makes a slice from a pointer and a length: To learn how to get memory, see Allocators.

description: if, while, for, switch and defer.

heading: for
text: A for loop walks over an iterator. it_range(n) gives numbers from 0 to n - 1: You can also get the index: A for loop is a short way to write this: So to make your own iterator,write your own iterator_next and iterator_current functions for your iterator type.

heading: switch
text: There is no fall through. Each case stops at the next case. The default case: is required, unless you switch over an enum:

heading: defer
text: defer runs an expression at the end of the current scope. Use it to free things right next to where you made them: If there are many defers, they run in reverse order.

description: Declare functions, use default arguments, overloading, function pointers and C functions.

heading: Declaring a function
text: The return type comes after :. If there is none, the function returns void.

heading: Functions inside functions
text: You can declare a function inside another one. It is only visible there: There is no closures or lambdas in Mox, so inner function does not see variables of outer function.

heading: Overloading
text: Functions can have the same name with different arguments: The compiler picks the best match among the functions it can see from the call. If a module with the right version is not imported, the compiler will not find it.

heading: Function pointers
text: A function pointer type is written as *fn (args): result:

heading: Calling C functions
text: #linkc declares a function from C. Write only the signature: If you want a different name in Mox, put the C name in brackets: #linkc on a function with a body gives it a C name, so C code can call it. That is why main is written like this:

heading: Caller location
text: A parameter with the default value #caller_location gets the place in the source where the function was called. Useful for logs and asserts: The file path is only there if you build with embed_source_paths=true (or -g).

description: Import other files, name imports, and re-export from a module.
text: Each .mox file is a module.

heading: Importing
text: A path that starts with ./ is relative to the current file. Any other path is looked up in the modules folder next to the compiler. Modules can import each other in a circle. This is allowed.

heading: Named imports
text: Give a module a name to keep its names apart:

heading: What is visible
text: Names from an imported module are visible only in the file that imports it. If a.mox imports b.mox, and main.mox imports a.mox, then main.mox does not see b.mox. To make a "root" module that gives all names from its parts, add #export: Now import "./all.mox"; gives you the names from both parts. This is how std.mox works: one import gives you the whole standard library.

heading: Built-in modules
text: Some useful modules in the modules folder: std.mox - printing, strings, memory, containers, file system, OS build.mox - helpers for build steps, like copying files next to the output vendor/raylib.mox, vendor/sdl3.mox, vendor/box3d.mox, vendor/microui.mox - ready bindings for these C libraries

description: Write functions and structs that work for many types, using compile time parameters.
text: Think of generics as templates. A generic parameter is a value that is known at compile time. For each new value, the compiler makes a new copy of the function or struct.

heading: Compile time parameters
text: A parameter whose name starts with $ is known at compile time. Inside the function it works like a constant. When its type is __type_ptr, it holds a type: A generic function must always have its return type written. Any type can be used for a $ parameter, not only types:

heading: Finding parameters from the argument
text: The compiler can find $ parameters from the type of an argument. Here $T and $SIZE come from what you pass: You can also capture the whole type with $Name / pattern: Here $PtrT is the full type *Buffer(...), and y must have the same type.

heading: Types are values
text: A type is a value of type __type_ptr. You can store it in a constant and pass it around: Sometimes the compiler reads a type as an expression and gets confused. Wrap it with #type:

heading: Reading type info
text: A __type_ptr can be cast to *MoxType to read type info, like its size:

heading: Overloading and generics together
text: Generics, overloading and default arguments work together. You can have one normal version of a function and one generic version with the same name. The compiler picks the best match.

description: Design types so that all-zero memory is a valid, ready to use value. No constructors needed.
text: ZII means "Zero Is Initialization". The idea is simple: when all bytes of a value are zero, the value is already valid and ready to use. You do not need a constructor or an init function. Mox does not have constructors, so ZII is the main way to make values that are easy and safe to create.

heading: Zero works for every type
text: = 0 sets every byte of a value to zero. It works for any type: You can also reset a value back to zero later:

heading: Why it is useful
text: Less code. Make a value with = 0 and use it. No init call to forget. Fast. Zeroing memory is one of the fastest things a computer can do. Memory you get from the OS is often zero already. Easy reset. x = 0 puts any value back to its start state. This works for one value or a whole array of thousands. Fewer bugs. A zero value is always the same, so there are no random values from old memory.

heading: Designing types for ZII
text: ZII does not happen by itself. You design your types so that zero means something good. Some simple rules:

heading: Zero means "empty" or "none"
text: A length of 0 is an empty list. A null pointer means "there is nothing here":

heading: Put the default enum value first
text: The first enum value is 0. Make it the default or "none" state:

heading: Name bools so false is the default
text: false is zero. So name a bool for the less common case:

heading: Start ids from 1
text: If you use numbers as ids or handles, keep 0 for "no id". Real ids start from 1:

heading: Set things up on first use
text: If a type needs something that zero can not give, set it up when it is first needed. Here a zero IntList gets its allocator on the first push: Using it needs no init at all:

heading: Functions accept zero values
text: Functions that read a value should work on a zero value too. For example, the length of a zero list is 0, and freeing a zero list does nothing.

heading: Zero in the standard library
text: DynArr from the standard library follows this in part. A zero DynArr is a valid empty array: But it needs an allocator before you add items, so call dynarr_init before push. See Allocators.

heading: Setting only some fields
text: A struct literal must list all fields. To set only a few, start from zero and then set them:

heading: Zeroing allocated memory
text: Memory from mem_alloc is not zeroed. Zero it yourself:

heading: When not to zero
text: If you are going to fill a big buffer anyway, zeroing it first is wasted work. Use #memory_garbage to skip it: Only do this when you are sure every byte will be written before it is read.

description: Allocate and free memory with allocators, and swap the allocator for code you call.
text: Mox has no garbage collector and no destructors. You get memory and free it yourself. Because memory is just bytes, you can reuse the same memory for different types. The standard library gets memory from allocators and arenas.

heading: The current allocator
text: Each thread has a current allocator. Get it with get_context_alloc(). The default one is created the first time you ask for it.

heading: Allocate and free
text: mem_alloc takes a type or a size in bytes. defer right after the allocation makes sure the memory is freed at the end of the scope.

heading: Containers keep their allocator
text: Every container remembers the allocator it was made with. For example, DynArr (a growing array): Using it:

heading: Swap the allocator
text: Because containers keep their allocator, you can change the current allocator for some code, and it will use yours: You can also go back from such an allocator to its arena:

description: Use arenas and temp buffers for fast short-lived memory.
text: An arena is a big block of memory. You push data into it one piece after another. You do not free pieces one by one. Instead you reset the whole arena at once. This is the best way to work with temporary memory. It is fast and you can not forget to free something.

heading: Temp arenas
text: The standard library has a few scratch arenas per thread. #temp_arena() takes one and resets it at the end of the current scope:

heading: Avoiding conflicts
text: Sometimes a function gets an arena as an argument and also needs its own temp memory. If both use the same scratch arena, the temp memory can overwrite the result. To avoid this, pass the other arena to #temp_arena. It will pick a different one:

heading: Temp buffers
text: #temp_buffer is a short way to get temporary bytes: #temp_c_string makes a temporary C string (with zero at the end) from a slice:

heading: Full example
text: This function reads a line from the console. It uses a temp buffer for reading, then copies the result into the arena the caller passed:

description: Use
text: Any Mox code can run while the compiler works. This includes calls to C functions. This is called compile time (or "comptime") code.

heading: The #run directive
text: #run runs code while compiling: It can run a block too:

heading: Baking values into the binary
text: The result of #run is a normal value. Store it in a variable or constant, and it is written into the program: This works for files too. The file is read once while compiling, so the program has nothing to load at start: Constants always live at compile time. Since types are values, a type can be a constant too:

heading: Globals at compile time
text: The initial value of a global variable is evaluated at compile time, the same way as for const. You do not need #run for it. Even a function call runs while compiling, and only the result goes into the program: Compile time code can change global variables. But by default, when the program starts, each global goes back to its initial value. Add #no_comptime_reset to keep what compile time code wrote into it: This lets you collect data while compiling and use it when the program runs. See Compiler hooks for a full example.

heading: What can go from compile time to runtime
text: Not every value can be passed from compile time to the running program: Numbers, bools, structs and arrays of them - yes. Slices - yes. The memory they point to is copied into the program. Function pointers - yes. They point to the same function in the program. Raw pointers (*T) - no. A raw pointer is just an address inside the compiler, and the compiler does not know how much memory is behind it. So if you build data at compile time and want to keep it, store it as a slice, not as a raw pointer:

heading: Am I running at compile time?
text: Since any function can run at compile time, sometimes it needs to know:

heading: Speed
text: Compile time code mostly runs in an interpreter, so heavy code can be slow. On the jit backend, the interpreter can call jit-compiled functions, which is much faster.

description: Read env variables, run shell commands, use
text: Mox has no separate build system. The build logic is normal Mox code that runs at compile time. This page follows examples/3_comptime.mox.

heading: Bake the git hash
text: os_exec_output runs a command and returns what it printed. With #run this happens while compiling, so the hash is stored in the program:

heading: Conditional compilation with #if
text: #if checks a compile time value. The branch that is not taken is not compiled at all: You can chain it: #if (a) { } else #if (b) { }. To check the OS, use MOX_OS:

heading: Build a C library and call it at compile time
text: This is the fun part. While compiling, the code below: builds a small C library with clang, loads it into the compiler, copies it next to the final program, calls its function at compile time. __compiler_link_lib(path, true) loads the library into the compiler.So comptime_example can be called right away inside #run. build_copy_to_output from build.mox copies a file next to the output executable.

description: Treat code as a value with
text: In Mox, code itself can be a value. You can keep it, build it, and insert it somewhere. The compiler then treats it as if you wrote it there by hand.

heading: Code as a value
text: #ast takes a piece of code without running it. Its type is __ast_ptr:

heading: Inserting code
text: #land_ast puts the code where it is written:

heading: Emitting code from a loop
text: Inside #run, #emit adds code to the place where #run is. It can use compile time values like the loop variable: This unrolls the loop: the program gets 10 lines, total += 0;, total += 1; and so on. #for is a short way to write the same thing:

heading: Code from a string
text: __compiler_parse turns a string into code:

heading: Example: constants from a config file
text: A function can build the string at compile time from any data. Here we read a config file and make a constant for each line. config.txt, next to the source file: The code: How it works: fs_read_file_full reads the file. This happens while compiling. split_iterator walks over the lines, and index_of finds the = in each one. A StringBuilder collects the code. For this file it is: __compiler_parse turns the text into code, and #land_ast puts it into the module. Now width and height are normal constants. The program does not read config.txt when it runs. Change the file and build again to get new values.

heading: When to use it
text: Use it when names or values in your code come from data: a config file, a table, a list of names. It is also good for picking code per platform. For simple cases, generics or macros are easier to read. For example with code generation #soa is implemented this way.

description: Write macro functions that expand in the caller, share names with the caller, and take code as an argument.
text: A function whose name starts with # is a macro. Its body is put into the caller, instead of being called.

heading: A simple macro
text: The array lives in the caller's scope, so the returned slice is valid until the end of that scope. A normal function could not do this.

heading: Names are hidden by default
text: Variables inside a macro are not visible to the caller. So a macro can not break the caller's variables by accident. These are called hygienic macros.

heading: Sharing with the caller
text: Put a backtick ` before a name to make it visible to the caller: The backtick works for defer and control flow too. They then act in the caller's scope:

heading: Example: fail and return
text: From examples/4_sdl3.mox. On error, it prints a message and returns -1 from the function that used it:

heading: Taking code as an argument
text: A macro can take code (__ast_ptr) and insert it with #land_ast: it comes from the macro with a backtick, so the code you pass can use it.

heading: Aliases
text: #alias name = expression; gives a name to an expression. It can be in a module, in a function or in a struct: The expression is compiled where the alias is declared, not where it is used. So unlike C defines, it can not see the caller's variables. Aliases could slow compilation, because the expression is compiled again each time it is used and also makes code less predictable. Use them only when you really need them.

description: Run your code after the whole program is compiled, to collect data and pass it to runtime.
text: A hook is your code that the compiler calls at some moment.

heading: The compilation ended hook
text: MOX_COMPILER_HOOK_COMPILATION_ENDED is called after all modules are compiled, but before the final code is written. At this moment your code can still change global variables or add more code. Register a hook with a macro function and one pointer argument:

heading: Example: a command list
text: This is examples/5_comptime_command_list.mox. Functions register themselves at compile time. When compiling ends, the list is saved into a global, and the program uses it when it runs. Output: Two things make this work: commands has #no_comptime_reset, so the value set at compile time stays when the program runs. See Globals at compile time. commands is a slice, and function pointers taken at compile time are valid at runtime too. Raw pointers would not work here, see What can go from compile time to runtime.

heading: Other ideas
text: The same hook can walk over a list of resources and process them before the program is built. For example: pack all textures into one atlas, compress it, and fix the coordinates in the list.

description: Open a window and draw with raylib, then run the same window at compile time.
text: Mox comes with ready bindings for raylib, a simple library for games and graphics. You do not need to install anything. The library files are in modules/vendor/raylib. This page follows examples/2_raylib.mox.

heading: Open a window
text: The raylib functions have the same names as in C. If you know raylib, you already know how to use it from Mox.

heading: Build
text: The raylib library file is copied next to the executable for you, so you can run it right away.

heading: How linking works here
text: vendor/raylib.mox imports vendor/raylib/link.mox. That file runs at compile time. It picks the right library file for your OS, adds it to the linker command, and copies it to the output folder: You can use the same idea for your own C libraries. See Linking.

heading: A window at compile time
text: Since any code can run at compile time, you can open the raylib window while compiling. You only need to load raylib into the compiler first: The window opens during the build. When you close it, the compiler goes on. This is not very useful for a real program, but the same trick lets you make tools that run inside the build, like a level editor or an asset preview.

heading: Bigger examples
text: examples/asteroids.mox - a small asteroids game with raylib. examples/box3d.mox - 3D physics with box3d, drawn with raylib. examples/microui.mox - a UI made with microui, drawn with raylib. All of them build the same way:

description: Create an SDL3 window and renderer, handle events, and use a macro for error handling.
text: Mox also comes with bindings for SDL3. The bindings were made from the SDL headers by a tool, so all names are the same as in C. The library files are in modules/vendor/sdl3. This page follows examples/4_sdl3.mox.

heading: Error handling with a macro
text: SDL functions return a failure value and keep the error text in SDL_GetError(). This macro prints both and returns -1 from main: from_c_string turns a C string (*u8) into a slice ([]u8).

heading: Window and renderer
text: Each thing we create gets a defer right after it. So everything is cleaned up in the right order, even when #fail returns early:

heading: The main loop
text: event uses #memory_garbage because SDL_PollEvent fills it anyway. To read the event type, the pointer is cast to *SDL_CommonEvent, the part that all events share.

heading: Build
text: The SDL3 library file is copied next to the executable.
